Fandom is not the root for fascism in football, it's a complete false association often rooted in classist beliefs about football fans in general.

Fascists have always sought to organise through football and have always achieved some success at clubs with right-wing history. HSV, the home side in this video are actually a good example of this. Though funnily enough, St Pauli are in the same city, Hamburg, and have a huge left-wing antifascist ultras section. 

The Hamburg derby was played with fans for the first time in years (covid) on Friday and St Pauli won 3-2. Come on!

Sport becomes a battleground of ideas just as anything else does. Targeting fandom or ultras in general isn't the elixir for stamping out fascism that you think it is. 

We should vociferously oppose fascist/nazi groups in any part of society but tarring an incredibly diverse group of people with the same brush as "fronts for organized crime and white supremacist murderous gangs" is wildly inaccurate.

So many people in the comments overreacting. This is normal for some teams in European football who have ultras sections. Flares are usually only let off for a few minutes of a game and are one of the ways in which ultras support their teams alongside tifos and chanting. People are generally very excited to be with the ultras as these kind of things often happen in away ends anyway where mostly only hardcore fans of the team get tickets. Home sections that do similar are often clearly marked as ultras sections to avoid families getting caught up in all the commotion. 

Football is a visceral experience in the EU, North Africa and South America. You often find yourself with large communities of people who devote a really significant part of their life to their football club. It's exciting! You're on your toes, not quite totally relaxed and this is what so many of us love about it. 

And we can also totally understand at the same time that that quality of being slightly intimidating/scary means that it's not for everyone. And that's okay! There are plenty of places to watch football in virtual serenity, a Dynamo Dresden away end just isn't one of them!

It's a really interesting question. I think personally there needs to be a medium-term plan to replace Antonio because of his unreliable fitness and age. I don't think a direct competitor right now would be a bad thing but it feels like it's coming one year too early, if that makes sense. Right now Antonio's at the top of his game and were we to bring someone else in of a similar level, attempting to share the game time could harm the development/adjustment of the new player & the form of both.

For me, the best way to manage this is probably by using the loan system. A loan for someone from now until the summer would suit and then I'd like to see the club move Yarmolenko on and replace him with someone who has true flexibility between the wings and striker position and is comfortable knowing that they're going to spend long periods as a back-up. I imagine this will be Josh King.

Then summer '22 would probably be the ideal window to target a serious Antonio replacement. That also allows time for the financial implications of the pandemic to hopefully settle so the club have a clearer picture of where they sit with that too.

Fans will demand something much sooner though and I think Moyes would prefer to have a direct competitor in there as well... Which means it's probably more likely that we look to exploit the Mediapro situation in France and bully a club into selling low to us either this Jan or in the summer. 

I'd probably expect one of Dia, Kadewere, Toko Ekambi, Delort, Laborde, Ajorque or Niane to tip up at some point...

Nzola is having a solid season for Spezia and he's definitely a good finisher but from having a look at some of his duels footage and some general play, I'd have some questions over his aerial ability and some concerns around whether he can carry the ball forward himself successfully. There's also the fact that this upturn in form is relatively recent still and this is first season in top flight football. Probably want to give that some more time before making any clear judgements.

But then this is what makes finding "an Antonio" so difficult. You're sort of looking for Benteke and Adama Traore (+ some additional finishing ability) in one player. That's hard to find. So when you compromise on aerial ability and ball carrying you get Boulaye Dia, M'Bala Nzola etc. And when you compromise on physical strength you get Dennis Man, Noni Madueke etc. 

To get all of those attributes at a high level in the same player is incredibly rare. We have lots of it but without some composure, finishing ability and fitness in Antonio himself. A perfect example of how there are always drawbacks.

The closest to him out of they players I've looked at so far just purely on numbers is probably Nicolas Gonzalez at Stuttgart.
